title: The Soviet Union invades eastern Poland
subtitle: The second invasion and the closing roads
body:
Before dawn on 17 September 1939, the Polish ambassador in Moscow was asked to accept a document that declared his country effectively dead. Wacław Grzybowski refused. Poland’s armies were still fighting, its capital had not surrendered, and its government was still on Polish territory. Within hours, Soviet troops were crossing the frontier. The invasion began with an attempt to make the state being invaded disappear on paper before its soldiers had stopped resisting.

The note presented to Grzybowski made the Soviet argument in a carefully arranged sequence. Poland’s government had broken down; the state had consequently ceased to exist; agreements with that state had therefore lost their force. Ukrainians and Belarusians in eastern Poland supposedly required protection, and the Red Army would provide it. The American ambassador’s contemporary report preserves this explanation as Moscow issued it. It records a justification for an invasion, not an impartial account of conditions in Poland. [1] [2] For Polish soldiers and civilians, the practical question was more immediate. Much of the country was already exposed to the German offensive described in the [previous chapter](/articles/german-invasion-poland-1939-09-01). The east contained military depots, replacement units, roads towards neutral neighbours and people who had fled the fighting farther west. Soviet intervention brought another army into this remaining space. It threatened the possibility of regrouping, but also the simpler hope that continuing eastward would lead a family away from the war. The [agreement of 23 August](/articles/molotov-ribbentrop-pact-1939-08-23) explains why Berlin and Moscow could contemplate dividing Poland. The surviving September correspondence shows how that understanding became an operation: through arguments over timing, instructions about aircraft, and negotiations over the words each government would use. On the Polish side, the same days produced decisions about withdrawal, resistance and surrender, often made with incomplete information. Reading those histories together reveals an invasion planned in considerable detail whose consequences were experienced in profound uncertainty.

A pretext prepared in advance

Moscow’s public explanation was being discussed with Germany a week before Soviet troops crossed the border. On 10 September, Foreign Commissar Vyacheslav Molotov told the German ambassador, Friedrich-Werner von der Schulenburg, that the speed of Germany’s advance had surprised the Soviet leadership. Military preparations had to be accelerated. Molotov also explained the political story he intended to tell: Poland was collapsing, and the Soviet Union must protect Ukrainians and Belarusians threatened by Germany. According to Schulenburg’s report, Molotov considered that explanation necessary to keep the intervention from appearing aggressive. [3] This was an unusually revealing conversation. The claim of protection was being considered alongside the readiness of the attacking forces, before the alleged emergency had acquired its final public wording. Molotov even worried that a German–Polish armistice would complicate matters: if the fighting stopped, Soviet entry would look like the beginning of another war. The distinction mattered to him because appearances could affect diplomacy, domestic understanding and the international Communist movement. It did not alter what Soviet troops would be ordered to do when they crossed the frontier. On 14 September, Molotov said that military action could begin sooner than previously expected, but he wanted to know when Warsaw would fall. The capital’s capture would strengthen the claim that Poland had ceased to function. Soviet newspapers were already preparing the political explanation. Warsaw, however, continued to resist. The invasion would go ahead without the event that Moscow had hoped to use as its most convincing evidence. [4] Berlin wanted Soviet intervention, but objected to being cast as the danger from which the Red Army was rescuing its neighbours. On 15 September, Joachim von Ribbentrop instructed Schulenburg to explain that such language would present the two governments as enemies. His message also pressed for the date and hour of Soviet entry and for arrangements between military representatives. Germany’s interest was practical as well as political: Soviet action could spare German forces the task of pursuing the remaining Polish armies all the way towards the Soviet frontier. [5] At about two in the morning on 17 September, Stalin received Schulenburg with Molotov and Defence Commissar Kliment Voroshilov present. He announced that Soviet forces would cross that morning. The discussion included a proposed limit for German aircraft along the Białystok–Brest–Lwów line, intended to reduce the danger of clashes between the advancing armies. Stalin also read the diplomatic note intended for Poland and, according to the German report, altered three passages after Schulenburg objected. The telegram does not preserve the discarded wording; it does establish that Germany had an opportunity to influence the explanation before Poland received it. [6]

Inside the documents

Two different rounds of editing

The changes to the Polish note were followed by a separate negotiation over a joint German–Soviet communiqué. Interpreter Gustav Hilger’s memorandum records Stalin rejecting an unusually candid German draft and writing a replacement. The agreed statement, broadcast on 18 September, described the restoration of order and assistance to the Polish population. These were distinct documents, revised in separate conversations. Together they show how closely the public account was managed. [7]

The private purpose was therefore more specific than the public language suggested. Moscow was moving to occupy its agreed sphere while Polish resistance to Germany continued, and Berlin was accommodating that move. Their cooperation did not require a single command structure or the disappearance of mutual suspicion. It required compatible immediate objectives, advance notice and arrangements that allowed one invading army to approach the other. Those conditions were already being created while Poland was being told that intervention had become necessary because its own state no longer existed.

Orders, formations and directions

The military instructions make the planning visible. Directives 16633 and 16634, issued on 14 September over the names of Voroshilov and Chief of the General Staff Boris Shaposhnikov, ordered secret concentration, readiness by the end of 16 September and an offensive across the frontier at dawn on the 17th. They assigned commanders, forces, successive objectives and deadlines. Their language concerned defeating opposing troops. These were orders for an invasion, already prepared before the protective explanation was delivered. [8] [9] The northern offensive developed under the Byelorussian Front, commanded by Mikhail Kovalyov; the southern offensive under Semyon Timoshenko’s Ukrainian Front. A Soviet front was a command directing several armies across a broad theatre. The surviving orders are especially useful because they identify seven operational groups by their concentration areas. Those names allow us to follow the original assignments without treating later changes in army organization as though they had all been settled in the same document. The map therefore retains the group names used in the 14 September instructions. [10] The northern groups were to move towards the Wilno–Grodno region and the approaches to Baranowicze, while the southern groups were directed towards Volhynia, Lwów and the routes near Romania. Infantry divisions, cavalry divisions and tank formations appear together in the orders. The composition matters: this was an offensive by combined formations, with mobile elements intended to get ahead and prevent an opponent from reorganizing. A tank arrow on a map should not make the infantry, horses, artillery and supply columns behind it disappear.

The deadlines reveal the anticipated tempo more honestly than a single claim about kilometres advanced per day. The southern order expected the Shepetovka group around Równe and Dubno by the end of 17 September and at Łuck on the following day. Golikov’s group was given successive lines on the approach to Lwów. Tyulenev’s was directed towards the Strypa and then Stanisławów, with the wider purpose of cutting escape routes. These were ambitious marching and fighting schedules, dependent on roads remaining usable and resistance being overcome or bypassed. They cannot be converted into confirmed daily front lines. [9]

Reading the atlas

An arrow can show an intention

Open the 17 September map to see the seven planned directions. The lines are deliberately schematic. Their endpoints identify the direction of later objectives; they do not mean that Soviet troops stood there on the first evening. Front labels identify command sectors, not headquarters. The battles discussed below occurred over the following fortnight and remain dated separately in the campaign chronology.

This distinction is also essential to judging Soviet performance. A force could move rapidly through a lightly defended district and then encounter a serious obstacle at a bridge or city. The first achievement says little about the ease of the second. Poland’s military resources had already been drawn westward against Germany, giving the new invader an enormous advantage in the east. Yet the Red Army still had to turn a schedule into movement, movement into effective fighting, and military success into possession of places whose inhabitants had their own reasons to resist or remain afraid.

The Polish decision: fight, withdraw, or preserve the army

Reports of resistance reached foreign capitals almost immediately. On the morning of 17 September, the Polish ambassador in Paris told American ambassador William Bullitt that Soviet forces had entered northeastern Poland and that Polish troops were fighting them. The report is valuable precisely because it preceded the later simplifications. Border units did not all watch the invasion pass unopposed. News was arriving from separate places, through a state whose communications were damaged but whose diplomats and soldiers were still acting. [11] Marshal Edward Śmigły-Rydz’s response attempted to preserve what remained of Poland’s armed forces. He directed a general withdrawal towards Romania and Hungary and instructed troops to avoid combat with the Soviets unless attacked or subjected to disarmament. That qualification was crucial. The order was neither an invitation to join the Red Army nor an unconditional instruction to surrender. It sought to prevent an already hard-pressed army from exhausting itself against another vastly superior opponent while routes out of the country might still be available. [2] For a commander beside a frontier road, the distinction was difficult to apply. An approaching Soviet column might demand weapons, offer assurances or open fire. Avoiding a battle could preserve a unit, but accepting disarmament could end its ability to continue the war. Resistance could protect a crossing or a withdrawal, yet also expose soldiers to encirclement. These were incompatible dangers rather than stages in an orderly national plan. The later examples of Grodno, Lwów and the Border Protection Corps show commanders choosing differently as their circumstances changed. The government’s movement into Romania during the night of 17–18 September came after the Soviet invasion had begun. Its departure therefore cannot explain an attack publicly justified before it happened. Nor did crossing a frontier automatically extinguish the state or the allegiance of its armed forces. The immediate result was nevertheless disastrous for command: leaders attempting to continue their work abroad instead faced internment, while soldiers still inside Poland had to act amid rapidly narrowing options. Poland’s political and military continuation would have to be rebuilt outside the country. [12] The same reversal confronted refugees. People who had travelled east to escape Germany now found that their destination was becoming another occupied zone. The Holocaust Memorial Museum describes a flight conducted with whatever transport was available and often without a settled plan for where to stop. That uncertainty is worth preserving in the narrative. Families were not moving across the finished occupation map familiar to later readers; they were trying to determine which road was still open, where relatives might be found and whether the next border could be crossed. [13] Warsaw’s continued resistance made the Soviet claim of extinction particularly conspicuous, but the argument did not depend on the capital alone. A state under attack can lose communications, territory and freedom of action without consenting to its own disappearance. For Poland, the invasion was both another military emergency and a direct attack on that distinction. The Red Army’s orders treated Polish troops as an enemy to be defeated while Soviet diplomacy sought to remove the political entity on whose behalf they were fighting.

Where the advance met resistance

Wilno was fought over on 18–19 September. Grodno’s resistance followed on 20–22 September, with the principal fighting on the first two days and withdrawal continuing into the third. These dates matter because they show the invasion developing over time. Cities did not become Soviet possessions merely because they lay beyond the first frontier crossings. In each place, decisions about evacuation and defence intersected with the arrival of mobile Soviet forces. [2] Grodno illustrates the weakness concealed by a fast armoured approach. Much of its regular garrison had already been sent elsewhere. Major Benedykt Serafin helped organize a defence drawing on remaining servicemen and volunteers. On 20 September, tanks of the Soviet 27th Tank Brigade entered across the Niemen bridge without sufficient infantry support. Polish defenders used the weapons available, including petrol bottles at close range. Tanks inside streets could be attacked from positions their crews had difficulty seeing or reaching. Soviet reinforcements made the struggle increasingly unequal, and the main Polish forces withdrew during the night of 21–22 September. [14] The military lesson is more useful than a dramatic but uncertain tank-loss total. A river crossing concentrates movement; a street restricts observation and manoeuvre; infantry is needed to clear positions that an armoured vehicle can pass but cannot safely ignore. Grodno gave defenders opportunities that a comparison of national army strengths cannot convey. It also showed the limit of those opportunities. A local defence could impose losses and gain time without possessing the reserves needed to hold indefinitely against an enemy able to reinforce. The withdrawal led to further fighting near Kodziowce during the night of 21–22 September. The Polish 101st Reserve Uhlan Regiment, commanded by Major Stanisław Żukowski, encountered a Soviet mobile detachment associated with the 2nd Tank Brigade. The episode belongs to the history of cavalry operating against armour, but should not be reduced to a contest between a horse and a tank. It was a confused fight involving movement through villages and darkness, with Polish units trying to keep a route towards the Lithuanian frontier open. [15]

A soldier’s field of view

Three kilometres from a battle

Lieutenant Piotr Łazarewicz recorded that his exhausted company slept until seven on 22 September, unaware of fighting about three kilometres away. When it moved towards prepared trenches, those defences faced the Germans. His diary brings the campaign down to the scale of an officer receiving fragments of news, looking for cover and waiting for a messenger. His account of enemy losses came from another officer; it is not an independently checked tally. [16]

Farther south, General Wilhelm Orlik-Rückemann gathered surviving Border Protection Corps units into an improvised force. At Szack on 28–29 September, Polish troops fought their way through Soviet opposition, using concealed 37-mm antitank guns against approaching armour. Success opened a route towards the Bug, but it did not solve exhaustion, supply shortages or the danger beyond the next crossing. At Wytyczno on 1 October, renewed fighting ended with the decision to disperse the worn-down formation. The Polish Army Museum’s account follows this progression from concentration to tactical success and eventual dissolution. [17] These actions qualify the idea of a bloodless Soviet march without reversing the larger balance of power. Polish units could fight effectively and still lose the campaign because they lacked a secure rear, sustained supply and a strategic destination inside the country. A battle won on the road might buy another day of movement. It could not, by itself, reopen the country around the men who had won it. The experience was therefore one of repeated decisions about what could still be saved.

Lwów and the value of a promise

Lwów confronted the Soviet advance while already defending itself against Germany. German attempts to seize the city had begun on 12 September and met resistance. On 18 September, the armoured trains Śmiały and Bartosz Głowacki reached the city; Soviet forward units attacked during the following night and were repulsed. The arrival of Śmiały provides a tangible connection with the first invasion chapter, where the train supported the fighting at Mokra. Equipment and men were still moving through Poland, even as the space in which they could operate contracted. [18] German forces subsequently withdrew from around Lwów under the arrangements between the occupying powers. For the defenders, that movement did not restore a secure rear or end the siege. It changed the immediate opponent with whom the city’s fate would be negotiated. General Władysław Langner accepted terms on 22 September that promised personal liberty and freedom of movement to Polish officers and protection of civilian property. Soviet authorities then violated those assurances and took Polish servicemen into captivity. [18] The sequence makes surrender a decision that needs explanation rather than hindsight. A commander faced responsibility for soldiers and civilians, limited prospects of relief and a choice between continued destruction and terms presented as a way out. We know what happened to the promises; he had to decide before their breach had occurred. Recognizing that uncertainty does not excuse the breach. It identifies the trust on which a negotiated surrender depended and the power acquired by the party that chose not to honour it. Elsewhere, Soviet conquest also brought executions, arrests and the seizure of people associated with Polish authority. The Institute of National Remembrance documents killings of prisoners and defenders, including after the fighting at Grodno, alongside the developing machinery of detention. These actions were part of the immediate occupation, not merely consequences of later policies. The fate of captured officers would eventually lead into the history of the special camps and the Katyn murders of 1940; this chapter ends before that later crime, while recognizing the connection created by captivity in September. [19] What happened after surrender belongs in an account of military operations because it changed the meaning of the decisions made during them. Disarmament was not simply the removal of rifles from a map. It placed soldiers under an authority that could separate officers from their men, investigate their backgrounds and determine where they would be sent. The protective vocabulary of the invasion gave little guidance to a prisoner facing those decisions. His immediate safety depended on the conduct of the people who now controlled him.

Soldiers, civilians and incompatible expectations

Soviet soldiers entered Poland under instructions that described the operation as liberation from national and class oppression. Yet official language did not produce a single private response. A study published by the Institute of National Remembrance draws on Soviet political and police reporting to show enthusiasm, uncertainty and dissent. One recorded question from an officer before the invasion was whether sympathy should now lie with Poland or Germany. Such remarks reveal the difficulty of absorbing the sudden diplomatic turn; surveillance reports, however, cannot tell us how representative any particular opinion was. [20]

A changing explanation

Simonov’s remembered reaction

Konstantin Simonov later recalled sympathy for Poland when Germany attacked and then approval of Soviet intervention when it was presented as protection for threatened populations. He was a young correspondent in Mongolia, not an eyewitness to the Polish frontier crossings. His retrospective account is useful as one person’s recollection of how the official explanation could reconcile apparently conflicting feelings. It should not be treated as the voice of every Soviet soldier. [20]

The experience of the troops can also be approached through their assignments and encounters. Men sent forward under a liberation narrative could find themselves firing on Polish positions, facing petrol bottles in Grodno or approaching a city that had already repelled German attacks. The political meaning supplied from above did not remove the physical demands of the operation. Drivers still needed passable crossings; infantry still had to enter defended streets; commanders still had to decide whether their leading vehicles could proceed without support. The campaign exposed the distance between an easy explanation and a difficult encounter. Among civilians, national identity alone cannot explain every reaction. Eastern Poland contained communities divided by language, religion, property, politics and relations with the Polish state. Some people welcomed the incoming army; others hid, fled, resisted or waited to see what would happen. Stanisław Boridczenko’s study of Polish military accounts from Polesie and Volhynia finds sharply different reactions in neighbouring localities. It also emphasizes how officers’ assumptions and retrospective memories shaped what they recorded. Reports of attacks on Polish troops are evidence of particular acts, not a licence to assign collective guilt to an entire population. [21] One episode in that scholarship concerns the evacuation of military families from Pińsk to Dawidgródek. Orlik-Rückemann’s subsequent report described the move as protection from local hostility and judged that it had succeeded. The difference between two nearby places mattered more immediately to those families than a broad ethnic label. Other testimony distinguished violent armed groups from inhabitants who condemned them. The region contained collaboration, intimidation and assistance, sometimes close together; the invasion changed who could act openly and who needed protection. [21] Christoph Mick’s research on Lwów likewise warns against treating Polish, Ukrainian and Jewish recollections as interchangeable accounts of a shared experience. His comparison identifies conflicting experiences behind conflicting memories. For an atlas, the implication is practical: a city marker can identify a place, but cannot supply a single civilian reaction. A welcome given in one street, a threatened family in another and a soldier reporting hostility outside the city can all belong to the same history. They must be examined without allowing one episode to erase the others. [22] Jewish refugees faced a particularly dangerous comparison between the power they were escaping and the power arriving from the east. Flight from Nazi persecution could make Soviet entry appear to offer immediate safety, without implying approval of Soviet rule. Later arrests and deportations also affected Jewish refugees in the Soviet zone. The Holocaust Memorial Museum’s account follows people who remained, tried to cross another frontier or attempted to return to relatives in German-occupied territory. Decisions that look contradictory on a finished map become more comprehensible when separation, poverty and uncertain information are restored to the story. [13]

In London, Paris and Berlin

Polish diplomacy had no difficulty identifying the Soviet action as aggression. On the evening of 17 September, Bullitt reported that Poland’s ambassador in Paris had received Foreign Minister Józef Beck’s denunciation of the invasion. The ambassador also expressed bitter disappointment at the lack of effective British and French help and deep pessimism about Romania’s willingness to act. This was the view from a diplomatic post trying to obtain assistance while the military situation deteriorated faster than allied discussions could change it. [23] In London, the next day’s conversation between American ambassador Joseph Kennedy and senior Foreign Office official Alexander Cadogan revealed a different calculation. Cadogan did not consider Britain automatically at war with the Soviet Union under its agreement with Poland. He said the Polish ambassador had requested a formal protest but had not asked Britain to declare war. The same report records rejection of Moscow’s claim that the Polish government had ceased to exist. British officials could reject the justification while declining to enlarge the war. [24] That distinction offered little practical comfort to soldiers being disarmed in Poland, but it is necessary to understanding the Western response. Britain and France were already at war with Germany. Opening another war involved military and diplomatic consequences that their governments were unwilling to accept. Condemnation, continued recognition of Poland and effective assistance were separate questions. Poland required the last of these urgently; the first two did not reopen a road or stop a Soviet formation. Bullitt’s report from Paris on 20 September shows how far Western discussion had moved towards the next stage of the conflict. He described French expectations of possible German attacks in western Europe and concern about Romania. He also reported an extraordinarily long timetable for building the resources thought necessary for a successful offensive against Germany. These were contemporary assessments, not reliable predictions: the value of the document is the gulf it exposes between the timescale of Allied preparation and Poland’s immediate emergency. [25] At Brest on 22 September, German and Soviet commanders presided over a military ceremony as the German occupation gave way to Soviet possession. Heinz Guderian and Semyon Krivoshein appeared together there. The occasion made visible the cooperation described in the telegrams: the arrival of the second invading army could be arranged with the first, while the state whose territory they occupied had no voice in the transfer. [12] Berlin, meanwhile, dealt with Soviet intervention as something to coordinate. The September correspondence does not depict two powers independently rescuing populations from an accidental collapse. It records negotiations over their respective operations and the settlement that would follow. On 19 September, Molotov told Schulenburg that the earlier possibility of retaining a reduced Polish state had given way to a preference for partition. Even after the invasion began, the precise political outcome was still being discussed. Agreement on destroying Poland’s freedom of action preceded agreement on every detail of the territory to be taken. [26]

The invasion becomes an occupation

The political programme had also begun before the frontier crossing. A Byelorussian Front directive dated 16 September instructed officials to create temporary administrations including army and NKVD representatives, organize newspapers and arrange the transfer of landed property. It explicitly postponed the creation of collective farms. This was preparation to replace existing authority and reshape society, with the pace of particular measures adjusted to the immediate situation. The instruction is a useful corrective to the suggestion that administration developed only as an improvised response to disorder after the troops arrived. [16] Promises of protection could therefore operate at several levels at once. They explained the invasion to foreign governments, gave soldiers a political account of their mission and offered selected civilians expectations of security or social change. The authority enforcing those promises was an occupying army working with a political police organization. People who welcomed one promised change did not thereby gain control over the system being installed. Those who feared it could not assume that avoiding the fighting would leave their former lives intact. The end of September would bring a revised German–Soviet boundary agreement, the subject of the next chapter. Its line should not be projected backwards onto 17 September as though every district had already changed hands that morning. Between the frontier crossing and the diplomatic settlement lay resistance, withdrawals, surrenders, captivity and decisions about escape. The distinction between those processes is the reason this atlas separates operational arrows from territorial boundaries. [27] For Poland, the invasion’s decisive effect was to close possibilities while people were still trying to use them. A commander could win a local fight and discover that the route beyond it was threatened. A civilian could escape the German advance and arrive under Soviet occupation. An officer could negotiate terms and find that the authority granting them did not intend to observe them. None of these experiences can be conveyed adequately by colouring eastern Poland and moving directly to the next treaty. On 17 September, the Soviet Union attacked a country whose defeat it publicly described as already complete. The evidence of advance planning, military orders and diplomatic coordination exposes the convenience of that description. The evidence of continued Polish resistance exposes its falsity. Between those two bodies of evidence are the people who had to live through the invasion: soldiers learning what their orders meant at a defended bridge, commanders trying to preserve their men, and civilians discovering that the direction in which they had sought safety no longer promised it.
author: Ostfront Atlas
location: Eastern Poland, Moscow and the European capitals
summary: Behind Moscow’s protective explanation stood a prepared offensive. Polish soldiers and civilians faced shrinking choices as Soviet formations advanced, resistance continued and promises of safety gave way to occupation.

sections.label: The Polish decision: fight, withdraw, or preserve the army
Lwów and the value of a promise

sourceMethod: Contemporary Soviet orders are read alongside German and American diplomatic reports, Polish military scholarship, museum research and testimony. Orders establish intended objectives, not actual daily positions. Transcriptions identify archival references but were not checked against original manuscript images. Reports and memoirs preserve particular perspectives; surveillance records are not opinion polls. Mick’s article is used only through its accessible abstract. Later battles are dated explicitly, uncertain casualty totals are omitted, and source notes record important limitations. Analysis connecting these findings is the atlas’s own interpretation.
